## Inner Product

:::{.definition data-title="Inner Product"}

Given [[vector-spaces|linear vector space]] $\mathcal{V}$ an 
**inner product** $\left< \cdot, \cdot \right>:\mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{V} 
\to \mathbb{R}$ is a mapping satisfying the following properties for all 
$v_{1}, v_{2}, v_{3} \in \mathcal{V}$:

1. Symmetry: $\left< v_{1}, v_{2} \right> = \left< v_{2}, v_{1} \right>$;
2. Non-negativity: $\left< v_{1}, v_{1} \right> \geq 0$;
3. Non-Degeneracy: $\left< v_{1}, v_{1} \right> =0 \iff v_{1}=0$; and
4. Linearity: $\left<  \alpha v_{1}, v_{2} + v_{3} \right> = 
   \alpha \left<  v_{1}, v_{2} \right> + \alpha \left< v_{1}, v_{3} \right> = 
   \alpha \left<  v_{1}, v_{2} + v_{3} \right>.$

:::

**Note:** Every **inner product** creates a **norm** satisfying: 
$\lVert v \rVert = \sqrt{ \left< v, v \right> }.$

## Inner Product Space

:::{.definition data-title="Inner Product Space"}

A vector space with a corresponding inner product is known as an 
**Inner Product Space**.

:::

:::{.definition data-title="Complete Inner Product Space"}

An inner product space is said to be **complete** if every [[cauchy-sequence]] 
$\{v_{n}\}$ in the inner product space, there exists a limit
$v \in \mathcal{V}$ such that $\lim_{n \to \infty} v_{n} = v$.

:::

A complete inner product space is known as a [[hilbert-spaces|Hilbert space]].

### Inner Product Space Results

Some important inner-product space results include:

1. The [[cauchy-schwartz-inequality]]: $\lvert \left< v_{1}, v_{2} \right> 
   \rvert\leq \lVert v_{1} \rVert \cdot \lVert v_{2} \rVert$.
2. The [[triangle-inequality]]: $\lVert  v_{1}+v_{2} \rVert \leq \lVert v_{1} 
   \rVert + \lVert  v_{2} \rVert$.


## Bilinear Forms

:::{.definition data-title="Bilinear Form"}

A function $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:\mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{V}\to F$ on a vector
space $(\mathcal{V},F)$ is a **bilinear form** if it is linear in each argument:
$\langle\alpha\vec{x}+\vec{y},\vec{z}\rangle=\alpha\langle\vec{x},\vec{z}\rangle+\langle\vec{y},\vec{z}\rangle$
and $\langle\vec{x},\alpha\vec{y}+\vec{z}\rangle=\alpha\langle\vec{x},\vec{y}\rangle+\langle\vec{x},\vec{z}\rangle$.
It is **symmetric** if $\langle\vec{x},\vec{y}\rangle=\langle\vec{y},\vec{x}\rangle$ and
**positive definite** if $\langle\vec{x},\vec{x}\rangle>0$ for all $\vec{x}\neq\vec{0}$.

:::

Every bilinear form on $\mathbb{R}^n$ has the form $\langle\vec{x},\vec{y}\rangle_A=\vec{x}^\top A\vec{y}$
for a unique $A\in M_n(\mathbb{R})$, and conversely every such $A$ defines one. The
form is symmetric if and only if $A$ is symmetric, and positive definite if and
only if $A$ is [[matrices#Quadratic Forms and Positive Definiteness|positive definite]].
Thus an **inner product on a real vector space is exactly a symmetric positive
definite bilinear form**.

## Euclidean Space

:::{.example data-title="Euclidean Space"}

On $\mathbb{R}^n$ the **dot product** $\langle\vec{x},\vec{y}\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^nx_iy_i$
is an inner product (the matrix $A=I_n$). It induces the **Euclidean norm**
$\lVert\vec{x}\rVert=\sqrt{\langle\vec{x},\vec{x}\rangle}=\left(\sum_ix_i^2\right)^{1/2}$,
the **metric** $d(\vec{x},\vec{y})=\lVert\vec{x}-\vec{y}\rVert$, and the **angle**
$\theta$ between nonzero vectors via
$\cos\theta=\frac{\langle\vec{x},\vec{y}\rangle}{\lVert\vec{x}\rVert\lVert\vec{y}\rVert}$.
The angle is well defined because of Cauchy-Schwarz below.

:::

## Cauchy-Schwarz and the Induced Norm

:::{.theorem data-title="Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality"}

For any $\vec{x},\vec{y}$ in an inner product space,
$$
\lvert\langle\vec{x},\vec{y}\rangle\rvert\leq\lVert\vec{x}\rVert\,\lVert\vec{y}\rVert,
$$
with equality if and only if $\vec{x},\vec{y}$ are linearly dependent.

:::

:::{.proof}
If $\vec{y}=\vec{0}$ both sides are $0$. Otherwise let
$\vec{z}=\vec{x}-\frac{\langle\vec{x},\vec{y}\rangle}{\langle\vec{y},\vec{y}\rangle}\vec{y}$. Then
$$
0\leq\langle\vec{z},\vec{z}\rangle=\langle\vec{x},\vec{x}\rangle-\frac{\langle\vec{x},\vec{y}\rangle^2}{\langle\vec{y},\vec{y}\rangle},
$$
which rearranges to the inequality. Equality holds iff $\vec{z}=\vec{0}$, that is,
$\vec{x}$ is a multiple of $\vec{y}$.
:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Induced Norm"}

$\lVert\vec{v}\rVert=\sqrt{\langle\vec{v},\vec{v}\rangle}$ is a [[normed-space#Norm|norm]],
and it satisfies the **parallelogram law**
$$
\lVert\vec{x}+\vec{y}\rVert^2+\lVert\vec{x}-\vec{y}\rVert^2=2\lVert\vec{x}\rVert^2+2\lVert\vec{y}\rVert^2.
$$

:::

:::{.proof}
Positivity and homogeneity are immediate. For the triangle inequality, by
Cauchy-Schwarz
$$
\lVert\vec{x}+\vec{y}\rVert^2=\lVert\vec{x}\rVert^2+2\langle\vec{x},\vec{y}\rangle+\lVert\vec{y}\rVert^2\leq(\lVert\vec{x}\rVert+\lVert\vec{y}\rVert)^2.
$$
The parallelogram law follows by expanding both squares, as the cross terms
$\pm2\langle\vec{x},\vec{y}\rangle$ cancel.
:::

The parallelogram law characterises the norms that come from an inner product.
For orthogonality, Gram-Schmidt and projections see
[[orthogonality-and-projections]].
